segments.title: Force K as a convoy-interdiction force
segments.summary: In 1941-42, Force K was a surface raiding force intended to stop Axis resupply convoys to North Africa outright. Malta's submarines and aircraft were already wearing that traffic down through attrition.
segments.body: The 1941 and 1942 versions of Force K had a different purpose from the 1939 formation. They were surface raiding forces aimed at freighters, using sea denial to make Axis resupply of North Africa unreliable. Submarines and aircraft operating from Malta could wear the traffic down over time, yet that attritional effect might still leave a trickle of supplies moving. A surface force could attack an entire convoy and stop the pipeline outright. The contrast explains why Force K mattered alongside Malta's air and submarine campaign.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts Malta-based attrition with a surface force stopping an entire Axis convoy pipeline.

segments.title: Force K's 1941 raiding group
segments.summary: The 1941 Force K paired the Arethusa-class light cruisers Aurora and Penelope with two L-class destroyers. The ships' fairly heavy anti-aircraft armament gave the raiders added security.
segments.body: Aurora and Penelope, both Arethusa-class light cruisers, formed the cruiser element of the 1941 Force K. A pair of L-class destroyers completed the small surface group. Together they could leave Malta and raid Axis convoy traffic directly. The ships carried fairly heavy anti-aircraft armament, which gave the force some security during its raids. This order of battle shows how a compact cruiser-destroyer group was organised for convoy interdiction.

evidence.note: The transcript's caption-damaged class name is read as Arethusa, followed by Aurora, Penelope, L-class destroyers, anti-aircraft armament, and raiding in 1941.

segments.title: Force K's 1942 cruiser-destroyer balance
segments.summary: In 1942, four 14th Flotilla destroyers and three Dido-class light cruisers formed a force capable of stopping almost anything likely to escort a convoy. Italian battleships were the exception.
segments.body: The 1942 Force K combined four destroyers from the 14th Flotilla with three Dido-class light cruisers. Its three cruisers and four destroyers could stop almost anything likely to escort a convoy. The formation's advantage depended on the level of protection assigned to the merchant ships. Italian battleships were the stated exception and would change the balance. The comparison sets Force K's operational limit: ordinary convoy escorts were within reach, while battleship cover was a different problem.

evidence.note: The transcript describes four 14th Flotilla destroyers, three Dido-class light cruisers, and the exception of Italian battleship escort cover.
